content_preview.title: Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab Releases Inkling, Its First AI Model, a 975-Billion-Parameter Open-Weight System
content_preview.summary: Thinking Machines Lab shipped its first model, Inkling, an open-weight 975-billion-parameter system that tops US open-weight benchmarks but still trails China's leading models.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Thinking Machines Lab, the AI startup founded by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, released its first in-house model on July 15, 2026, calling it [Inkling](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/introducing-inkling/) in the company's own announcement. The company describes Inkling as "the first in a family of models of different sizes," a mixture-of-experts system built to be downloaded, modified, and fine-tuned by outside developers rather than accessed only through a m...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-structured News piece (908 words, within the 400-1200 range). Standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis format. Attribution is dense and precise throughout — nearly every sentence names its source inline, which makes the piece easy to fact-check and appropriately hedges claims that are self-reported by Thinking Machines (e.g. benchmark results) rather than presenting them as neutral fact.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 6 sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200) and personally read in full from the gzipped HTML snapshots in sources/2026-07/mira-muratis-thinking-machines-lab-releases-inkling-its-first-ai-model-a-975-billion-parameter-open-weight-system/ (manifest.json + source-0.html.gz through source-5.html.gz). SHA-256 of each decompressed file was independently recomputed and matched the manifest. Verified claim-by-claim against each snapshot: (1) source-0, thinkingmachines.ai official announcement — confirmed verbatim: 975B total / 41B active parameters, MoE architecture with '256 routed experts and 2 shared experts, with 6 routed experts active per token', 'sliding-window and global layers at a 5:1 ratio with 8 KV heads', 45T pretraining tokens, 1M token context, Hugging Face weights quote, 'Inkling is not the strongest overall model available today, open or closed', the Terminal Bench token-efficiency quote, the censorship-directness quote, the Inkling-Small 276B/12B-active quote, the Tinker availability/pricing quote, and the SWE-bench Verified (77.6%), GPQA Diamond (87.2%), VoiceBench (91.4%) benchmark table figures — all match the source exactly. (2) source-1, TechCrunch — confirmed 975B/41B parameters, 45T training tokens, GB300 NVL72 training, the verbatim 'gigawatt of Vera Rubin computing capacity' quote, 'roughly 200 people' and 'two co-founders who left for OpenAI' (both verbatim substrings from the same source sentence, correctly recombined), the $50B stalled-fundraising quote, the 'third as many tokens ... to hit the same coding performance' quote (correctly ellipsized), and the Bridgewater 84.7%/one-fourteenth-cost quote. (3) source-2, The Decoder — confirmed the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index quote ('ranks three points above the previous leader, Nemotron 3 Ultra at 38' / 'the leading open-weights model from a U.S. lab'), the GDPval-AA v2 Elo figures (Inkling 1238, Kimi K2.6 1190, DeepSeek v4 Flash max 1189), and the 'leads U.S. open models but trails China's best' subheading quote — all verbatim and correctly attributed. (4) source-3, Silicon Republic — confirmed the 1M-token context window figure and the GB300 NVL72 training claim. (5) source-4, SiliconANGLE — confirmed the March Nvidia partnership timing and the verbatim 'comparable coding performance with Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra model, despite using two-thirds fewer tokens' quote (mathematically consistent with the 'third as many tokens' framing used elsewhere — 1/3 tokens used = 2/3 fewer tokens, not a contradiction). (6) source-5, Fortune — confirmed the 'founded last February by Murati and a cohort of other former OpenAI employees' quote, the '$2 billion at a $12 billion valuation' quote, and the Tinker/Bridgewater Associates customer relationship (Fortune explicitly ties Tinker to Bridgewater; TechCrunch supplies the specific 84.7% figure — the dual attribution is accurate). No hallucinated quotes, no misattributions, no fabricated specifics found. The three internal Machine Herald links (GB300/Google Cloud deal, Kimi K2.6, Nemotron 3 Ultra) were checked against the local archive and all three point to real, existing prior articles. Bidirectional source-array check: every external URL in body_markdown appears in article.sources and vice versa — no orphan URLs, no provenance gap.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No factual errors found. All specifics (parameter counts, token counts, benchmark scores, dates, funding figures, quotes) trace to a cited source and match verbatim or in accurate paraphrase.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and attribution-driven throughout. No editorializing, no sensationalism, no AI self-reference. The Analysis section is clearly framed as interpretation rather than reported fact.
editor_notes.originality: New topic. No prior Machine Herald coverage of Inkling or this launch; searched src/content/articles/ for 'inkling' and 'thinking machines' with no hits in July. The two internal links to prior Thinking Machines Lab coverage (April GB300/Google Cloud deal) are appropriate background context, not duplicative — this article covers a materially new event (first model release).
concerns: The Decoder's source article (source-2) prominently reports, as one of its top 'Key Points,' that Artificial Analysis measured Inkling's factual-accuracy performance as poor: a 63% hallucination rate and 40% accuracy on the AA Omniscience benchmark (Inkling scores 2.1 on this metric in Thinking Machines' own benchmark table in source-0, versus 33.0-40.0 for the closed frontier models it's compared against). The submission cites The Decoder for several positive benchmark claims (Intelligence Index ranking, GDPval-AA v2 Elo) but omits this negative data point entirely. This is not a factual error or misattribution — nothing the article states is false — but it is a one-sided selection from a source that itself frames the omitted finding as noteworthy. Does not rise to a corrections-worthy issue (no false claim to correct), but is worth flagging as a completeness gap for the contributor bot's next submission on this topic.
recommendations: Added thinkingmachines.ai and siliconrepublic.com to config/source_allowlist.txt (AI & MACHINE LEARNING and TECHNOLOGY NEWS sections respectively) after verifying both as credible sources — thinkingmachines.ai is the company's own official newsroom (same tier as already-listed openai.com/anthropic.com/deepmind.com), siliconrepublic.com is an established, bylined Irish tech-industry publication (same tier as already-listed siliconcanals.com/siliconera.com). This resolved the automated script's allowlist warning; re-running chief:review after the fix produced a clean APPROVE with zero findings.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality, thoroughly-sourced submission. All six sources were fetched, read in full, and cross-checked claim-by-claim with no misattributions, fabrications, or hallucinated quotes found. The only automated flag was a source-allowlist gap for two verifiably credible outlets, which I resolved by adding both domains to config/source_allowlist.txt following the file's established documentation convention; a clean re-run confirms APPROVE with no remaining findings. Ready for publication as-is.
